_readme: THE LIST OF WHAT TO LOOK FOR, shipped with the product. It is data: rewrite
it, extend it or switch it off without recompiling anything.
To add a tool: put a `.json` file in `~/.config/sailor/tools.d/` (or wherever
SAILOR_TOOL_DESCRIPTORS points) holding an array of descriptors, or an object
with a `tools` field. An `id` already present in here is replaced by yours;
to remove one, rewrite its `id` with `"disabled": true`.
A descriptor has `detect` (this thing is either here or not) or `enumerate`
(the entries are discovered by reading a configuration file), never both.
`detect` is one probe or a list of probes: `{"command": "name"}` looks for an
executable on the search path, `{"path": "~/x/*.json"}` sees whether a file
is there. One answering is enough.
`version` says how to ask the executable found for its version; it must be a
question, not a gesture: the detection really runs it. `config` says where its
configuration lives. `~/`, `$VAR` and `*` work in every path.
`ask` says how a one-shot question is put to an engine, so that a step need
not know anybody's options: `args` are the options without the question's
text, `prompt` says where that text goes (`stdin` or `last_arg`), and
`unusable_when` lists the words that engine uses to declare it CANNOT work —
quota spent, credentials missing. Only those move a step on to the next engine
in its chain: declare the provider's own words, never a generic rule like
«error», or a wrong brief would travel the whole chain until somebody answers
anyway. An engine without `ask` stays usable, but only from a step that writes
the options itself.
`exhausted_when` names, among the words of `unusable_when`, those that mean the
QUOTA is spent rather than a credential missing: the step closes with the
exhaustion class, the ledger row says `quota_exhausted`, and `cooldown_secs`
sets the engine aside that long so a chain does not knock again on a door
known to be shut. Empty means nobody has told the two apart — never «it never
runs out». A word here that no word of `unusable_when` covers is a
contradiction the loader names: the run would read it and the dry run would
not, and the same output would get two verdicts.
`refuses_without_prompt` lists the words that engine refuses the line
COMPOSED WITHOUT THE QUESTION with. It is how a real command line gets tried
at zero cost: with no question no provider is called, but the same argument
parsing as a real call runs, and a malformed line says so there instead of on
the first run that costs money. Declare the engine's words and not an exit
code: one measured engine exits 2 both when it refuses properly and when the
line is malformed, so the status does not tell the two apart and the text
does. Empty means «nobody looked», never «the line is sound».
`login_status` says how that engine is asked WHETHER THE HOME IT STARTS FROM
IS AUTHENTICATED, and it is needed because a declared and empty home applies
in silence: `sailor` can give each engine a credentials profile, and a profile
pointing at a directory with no credentials starts every call unauthenticated
with nothing to say so. `args` are the question's options (`["login",
"status"]`), and it MUST be a question and never a gesture: the check really
runs it, and `codex login` would open a browser. `logged_in_when` and
`logged_out_when` are the words that engine says yes and no with, and `answer`
is a pointer — the same one `usage` uses — for engines that do not answer in
prose: `claude` puts the answer in the boolean field `loggedIn` of a JSON
envelope, and `["loggedIn"]` reaches it. Without `answer` the subject is
everything the engine said, stdout and stderr together.
AND WHAT ENDS UP IN THE REPORT IS THE SUBJECT, NOT THE ENVELOPE. This is not
brevity: the real answer of `claude auth status` carries the owner's email
address, their organisation's identifier and name, and the subscription type,
and that text would end up in two outputs that get pasted into a handover and
poured into a log. Declaring an `answer` shows the isolated value — «false»
says the same thing without saying whose it is — and declaring none shows the
prose, which on the measured engines names nobody.
BOTH FORMS GET DECLARED, AND THE NO IS READ FIRST. «Not logged in» contains
«logged in»: the way of saying no is nearly always the way of saying yes with
a negation in front, and looking for the yes first would find an empty home
authenticated. The code imposes the order; whoever measures declares the right
words. An engine without the block triggers NOTHING: empty means «nobody
looked», never «it is authenticated», the same direction as
`refuses_without_prompt`. The check does not fail a run over a profile with no
credentials — punishing the innocent is the wrong cure — it just says so, in
`sailor flow check` and in `sailor profiles list`.
WHY `auth.json` ON DISK IS NOT INSPECTED. It would be a second copy of the
truth, rewritten per engine and kept aligned while engines move their things
around. And because the dry run is not enough: it tries the line WITHOUT the
question, so the engine stops before reaching the credential checks —
measured, `codex exec < /dev/null` answers the same with a full home and an
empty one.
`usage` says how THAT ENGINE'S CONSUMPTION is read, so that Sailor knows where
the money went with no code branch for any provider. `args` are the options to
add so it reports it (for example `["--output-format", "json"]`), `read` is
`json` or `text`, and the pointers say where the values are: `input_tokens`,
`output_tokens`, `cached_tokens`, `total_tokens`, `cost`, `model`, `answer`.
With `read: json` a pointer is a key path (`["usage", "input_tokens"]`); with
`read: text` it is a regular expression with the value in the first group.
THREE THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE WRITING ONE.
1. `cached_tokens` must be kept separate: tokens read from the cache cost an
order of magnitude less, and a single input number would make the
measurement false exactly where it counts.
2. If you set `args` that ask for a JSON envelope, you MUST declare `answer`
too, that is where the answer's text sits inside that envelope: without
it, the downstream step would receive the envelope instead of the answer.
Measuring must not change what is measured.
3. `model` is the only honest link to the price list
(`~/.config/sailor/pricing.json`): the name the engine declares is looked
up among the list's `id`s and `aliases`. Declaring none leaves the COST
unknown — never zero.
An example of the `json` form, to write in ~/.config/sailor/tools.d/ for an
engine whose keys you measured yourself on this machine:
"usage": {
"args": ["--output-format", "json"],
"read": "json",
"input_tokens": ["usage", "input_tokens"],
"output_tokens": ["usage", "output_tokens"],
"cached_tokens": ["usage", "cache_read_input_tokens"],
"cost": ["total_cost_usd"],
"model": ["model"],
"answer": ["result"]
An engine without `usage` works exactly as before, and leaves its tokens at
UNKNOWN. Not at zero: a zero in place of «I do not know» adds up, and no
downstream view can correct it any more.
`capabilities` says WHAT THAT ENGINE CAN DO BEYOND ANSWERING, and with which
arguments it is obtained. It is a map from name to declaration, and the code
knows none of those names: adding one means writing in here, never a
recompile. Each entry is written in one of three ways:
"choose_model": { "args": ["--model"], "takes_value": true }
"resume_session": [ {"args": ["--resume"]}, {"args": ["--continue"]} ]
"fork_session": false
A form has `args` (the options, or the subcommand), `takes_value` (the last
one wants a value straight after), `values` (the closed set, where one
exists) and `note` (the constraint the table cannot carry: «only with
--print»).
WRITING `false` IS NOT THE SAME AS STAYING SILENT, and that is why this block
has this shape. `false` says «somebody looked and it is not there»; a missing
line says «nobody looked». A block that only let you list what is there would
pass every absence off as measured, including that of a tool nobody ever
opened.
AN ENGINE THAT DECLARES NOTHING KEEPS WORKING. A missing capability is not an
error: an engine that cannot impose a shape on the answer asks for it in the
prompt and pays more tokens — which is how it always worked, and stays the
fallback. A step declares what it needs with `needs_capabilities`, and `sailor
flow check` warns, naming the step, the engine and the capability.
The names used here: `ask_without_interaction`, `response_shape`,
`resume_session`, `fork_session`, `isolate_from_user_config`,
`receive_equipment`, `native_spend_cap`, `choose_model`, `fallback_model`,
`read_remaining_quota`. The last is not a flag but a channel, and it is the
proof that the block holds for what is not on the command line too: it
declares that the tool can say how much quota the PERSON has already spent.
An engine without it keeps working without knowing — the usual fallback — and
one declaring it `false` is saying somebody looked, not that it is impossible.
They are not a closed list — nowhere in the code is one written down — but
inventing one beside an existing one gets you two descriptors talking about
two things nobody can compare.

login.note: measured with `claude auth --help`: `login` signs in, `status` asks; the browser opens from the terminal

quota.note: measured with an HTTP 200: `utilization` as a percentage per window and `resets_at`; a beta, versioned channel that can stop answering with nothing here changing, so a missing reading is a reading that is not there, never a zero

install.note: the native installer: on the machine measured, `claude` links to ~/.local/share/claude/versions/<version>, which is where that installer puts it

tools.label: Claude Code

refuses_without_prompt: input must be provided either through stdin

ask_without_interaction.note: `--print` is the long form of the same flag

response_shape.note: it takes a whole JSON schema, not a format name: the only one of the four that imposes the shape of the fields and not just the envelope

resume_session.note: the value is optional: without it, the picker opens
resumes the last conversation of this directory

fork_session.note: goes together with --resume or --continue: on its own it has nothing to fork

isolate_from_user_config.note: with an empty value the command line starts clean AND STAYS AUTHENTICATED: the user's skills disappear, the built-in ones remain. This is the form to use to equip an engine without writing in somebody else's home
isolates more and costs the credentials: without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY it answers «Not logged in», because OAuth and the keychain are not read

receive_equipment.note: repeatable; a directory or a .zip, for this session only
a JSON object, not a path

fallback_model.note: comma-separated list, tried in order; only with --print

read_remaining_quota.note: Not a flag: a channel. The OAuth token is in ~/.claude/.credentials.json under claudeAiOauth.accessToken, and https://api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage answers with the quota windows — `utilization` as a percentage and `resets_at` — given the header `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20`. Measured with an HTTP 200 response: five_hour at 2%, seven_day at 32%. It is the PERSON's quota across all their sessions, never the usage of one run. Read only, no cost. The reader is `models::remaining`.

reset_context.note: Typed into a session that is already running, not passed at launch. Established from the command list this command line publishes to its own sessions, NOT by running it and watching the context empty: the effect is on a live session, and measuring it means having one to spend. What is measured is that the line reaches the program — the conduit is provable without knowing what the line means. Whoever gets a chance to watch a real session empty should say so here and take this sentence out.

session_hooks.note: Measured on the installed binary, 01/09/2026. This is the line Sailor grew up grafted into, and the address used to be written into `session_cmd` with a comment arguing it was not a coupling because it was «the address of what we are grafting». The address IS the coupling: while it sat in the code, two other command lines that support the same four moments were grafted into nothing, and nothing said so.

tools.note: The words in `unusable_when` are the ones seen on a real machine: «You've hit your weekly limit · resets 7am». They are not a general rule, and must not be: if they change one day, the fallback stops firing and the step goes red with the real message — which is the right way to be wrong. The `usage` block is measured, and every key comes from a real output, not from documentation. TWO NON-OBVIOUS THINGS. (1) THE CACHE WRITE IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE ENTRY: in the measured call — two input tokens, four output — the 12,347 tokens written to cache were 96% of the 0.1285 dollars declared. The two durations have different prices and live in two different keys, so they are declared separately: adding them up would be a loss of information nobody would ever see again. (2) THE MODEL IS NOT A FIELD: claude uses it as the KEY of `modelUsage` (`{"modelUsage": {"claude-opus-5[1m]": {…}}}`), which is why the pointer takes the `first_key_of` form. Without that name no price-list entry is found, and the cost would stay unknown even with every count in hand. `refuses_without_prompt` is measured by composing the real line without the question: `claude -p --output-format json < /dev/null` exits 1 and prints «Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print». `login_status` is measured, and its shape is the reason the block has a pointer: `claude auth status` does not answer in prose but with a JSON envelope on STDOUT, and the answer is a BOOLEAN — `"loggedIn": true` in the real home, `"loggedIn": false` with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` pointed at an empty directory (where `authMethod` goes from «claude.ai» to «none»). The pointer `["loggedIn"]` is the same key path this descriptor declares the tokens' location with: no second mechanism. The command is local and calls no model. A NOTE THAT CONTRADICTS AN EARLIER MEASUREMENT: `claude auth status` exits **1** when not authenticated and **0** when it is, so here the status would tell them apart — but the verdict stays on the text, because the status is a fact about this engine and not a rule anyone can declare for all.

login.note: measured with `codex login --help`: `login` signs in through the browser, `login status` asks

tools.label: Codex

ask_without_interaction.note: a subcommand, not a flag: it wants to be first on the line

response_shape.note: it wants the PATH of a file holding the schema, not the schema

resume_session.note: the identifier is optional when --last is added

fork_session.note: the identifier is MANDATORY. Measured with `codex exec fork --help`: it does not appear among the options of `codex --help`, only among the subcommands of `exec`, which is why a reading of the options alone reports it absent

isolate_from_user_config.note: does not load $CODEX_HOME/config.toml; the credentials remain
does not write the session files to disk

receive_equipment.note: lays $CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml over the base configuration; the short form is -p, which on codex does NOT mean «print»
key=value, repeatable; the value is read as TOML

session_hooks.note: THE SAME EVENT VOCABULARY AS claude-code, measured on the binary 01/09/2026: it publishes PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop, Interrupt — all four of Sailor's moments among them. Both halves of the address are needed and neither alone: CODEX_HOME is unset in a plain shell, where the file is under the home, and points elsewhere under a host that declares it. No user words of its own were measured, so none is declared and the welcome must promise none.

tools.note: CODEX_HOME can move the configuration: the one you read by hand and the one its host passes it are not always the same. `exec` reads the prompt from standard input when it is not an argument (measured); the 401 in `unusable_when` is the one seen with expired credentials. The `usage` block has no `args`: codex already writes the tokens in its normal output, so measuring it changes neither the command line nor what the step receives. It declares only the TOTAL because that is all it says — it does not split input from output — and a cost cannot be derived from a total without inventing the proportion between the two sides: codex's cost therefore stays unknown, and its tokens do not. The shape of the line («tokens used», with the number on the next one and dots as separators) is the one measured on a real machine, the same one `models::usage::parse_codex_tokens` is tested on. `refuses_without_prompt` is measured: `codex exec --sandbox read-only < /dev/null` exits 1 and prints «Reading prompt from stdin...» followed by «No prompt provided via stdin.». Only the second line is declared: the first says it is waiting, not that it gave up. `read_remaining_quota` is `false` because it was TRIED AND FAILED, which is different from impossible — and here is how far it got, so whoever tries again does not start over. The method EXISTS in the published protocol: `codex app-server generate-json-schema --out DIR` lists `account/rateLimits/read` among the client requests, with `params` of type `null`. `initialize` answers instantly. The next request gets NO answer: tried twice, 45 and 50 seconds, with and without the `initialized` notification the protocol expects, and `account/read` does not answer either. No error, no refusal: silence. Still to try: the `app-server proxy` subcommand against the socket of the daemon already running, instead of a fresh process starting from scratch. And `~/.codex/state_5.sqlite` has `tokens_used` per thread, which is tokens spent, not quota left: not the same question. A note for whoever retries inside a sandbox: `codex app-server` wants to WRITE under `~/.codex`, and if it cannot it dies with «failed to initialize sqlite state runtime» — a write denial that presents itself as an engine fault. `login_status` is measured with both real homes: `CODEX_HOME=~/.codex codex login status` answers «Logged in using ChatGPT», and with `CODEX_HOME` pointed at one of the two profile directories without `auth.json` it answers «Not logged in». THREE MEASURED THINGS NOBODY WOULD GUESS. (1) It writes everything to STDERR, nothing to stdout: reading one pipe alone would never find either form. (2) Under a sandbox it prefixes a line of its own — «WARNING: proceeding, even though we could not create PATH aliases» — unrelated to the credentials, so the words are searched for inside the output rather than comparing it whole. (3) «Not logged in» CONTAINS «logged in»: hence the yes is declared as «logged in using», and hence `judge_login_status` reads the no first anyway — two defences, because the first depends on whoever writes the descriptor and the second does not. No pointer: the answer is prose, and the subject is everything the engine said. TWO EARLIER MEASUREMENTS CONTRADICTED, BOTH ABOUT EXIT CODES. (a) `codex login status` exits **1** unauthenticated and **0** authenticated: here the status would tell them apart. (b) `codex exec < /dev/null` exits **1**, not zero, and does so with both homes — the line claiming «exits zero» was false, while the conclusion resting on it holds, because that leans on the IDENTITY of the two answers and not on the number. Note that this same note, three sentences earlier, already declared «exits 1» for the same line: two sentences of one field said different things, a contradiction in miniature. The verdict stays on the text regardless: the status is a fact about this engine, not a rule that holds for whoever comes next.

login.note: no sign-in subcommand in `gemini --help`: the sign-in happens inside the program, on first start or with `/auth`

install.note: measured: /opt/homebrew/bin/gemini links to ../lib/node_modules/@google/gemini-cli/bundle/gemini.js; Homebrew also ships a `gemini-cli` formula

tools.label: Gemini CLI

ask_without_interaction.note: the short form is -p; the text goes in the option, not in a free argument

response_shape.note: IT CHOOSES THE ENVELOPE, NOT THE FIELDS: a closed set of three formats, not a schema. A step demanding a precise field shape from gemini must go on asking for it in the prompt

resume_session.note: «latest» or the index number, not a UUID
opens a NEW session with the given UUID: it does not resume one

isolate_from_user_config.note: it skips the trust prompt for the working directory, not the user's configuration: the weakest of the three isolations measured

receive_equipment.note: a list of extensions; without the option they are all loaded

session_hooks.note: ITS OWN NAMES FOR THREE OF THE FOUR, measured 01/09/2026: SessionStart keeps its name, UserPromptSubmit becomes BeforeAgent, Stop becomes AfterAgent, PreCompact becomes PreCompress. The handler has the same shape as everywhere else ({type: command, command, timeout}), which is why only the names are data here. Not guesswork: the vendor ships `gemini hooks migrate --from-claude`, the same table read the other way, and this block is what makes that translation unnecessary.

tools.note: The `capabilities` block is measured with `gemini --help`; the `ask` block on a real machine with gemini 0.57.0. The question goes IN AN ARGUMENT after `--prompt`, not on standard input: `-p/--prompt` is an option with a value, and the tool's documentation says that standard input text, when present, is APPENDED to it. `refuses_without_prompt` comes from the real line composed without the question — `gemini --prompt` exits 1 and prints «Not enough arguments following: prompt» — so it cost nothing and called no provider. TWO THINGS THAT ARE NOT HERE, AND ARE NOT OVERSIGHTS. (1) No `usage`: `--output-format json` wraps the answer, but where it puts the tokens was never measured, and declaring guessed pointers would leave the usage unknown while making the opposite look true. Without the block, gemini is invoked as it always was and its tokens stay unknown — which is the honest answer. (2) No `unusable_when`: how it declares itself exhausted has not been seen. So gemini CANNOT SIT IN THE MIDDLE OF A CHAIN: `Descriptor::cannot_be_a_fallback` says so, and the test `every_engine_that_is_not_last_in_a_chain_says_how_it_is_exhausted` goes red if anyone puts it there. That used to be the reason for not writing the `ask` block at all — that is, for leaving `ask_without_interaction` declared and unusable, which is a self-contradiction. NO `login_status` BLOCK, AND THIS IS WHAT WAS TRIED: `gemini --help` lists five subcommands — `mcp`, `extensions`, `skills`, `hooks`, `gemma` — plus the default query, and no options; across all 45 lines the words `auth`, `login`, `logout` and `credential` never appear. So there is no known way to ask it whether it is authenticated. That is not «it does not have one»: it is «I did not find it looking there», and the difference matters because the answer could live in a nested subcommand the top-level `--help` does not show — it happened with `codex exec fork`. Writing a guessed block here would be worse than the absence: one wrong word would declare an empty home authenticated, the very defect this block exists to close. A MERGE NOTE: the other branch, which wrote the paragraph above, opened this note with «No `ask` block» — true when written, false now: the `ask` was measured the same day on this branch, and the two sides were talking about the same field at two different moments. The measurement counts, not the absence.

login.note: no sign-in subcommand in `agy --help`: started without credentials it prints the OAuth URL and waits, as `unusable_when` records

tools.label: agy

unusable_when: Authentication required. Please visit the URL to log in

ask_without_interaction.note: the short form is -p; `--prompt` is an alias of the same thing. `takes_value` used to be absent — that is, said `false` — and said something untrue: `agy --mode plan --output-format json --print` answers «flag needs an argument: -print». It was the same truth written in two blocks that contradicted each other; corrected against the measurement, not the documentation

response_shape.note: it accepts the whole schema or the path of a file holding it

resume_session.note: the last conversation; the short form is -c

receive_equipment.note: adds a directory to the workspace, repeatable: it is all that can be handed to it from outside

tools.note: The `capabilities` block is measured with `agy --help`, and the four absences are written `false` on purpose: agy has no way to fork a session, to isolate itself from the user's configuration, to keep a spend cap of its own or to fall back on another model. «It does not have it» and «nobody looked» are two different facts, and omitting the line would say the second. The `usage` block is measured: agy counts the tokens and puts them in `usage`, but declares NEITHER the model NOR the cost — so its counts are recorded and the cost stays unknown, which is the honest answer. No key for the cache write: it declares none. WHERE IT KEEPS ITS OWN HOME, MEASURED: `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli`, under `$HOME` — agy is the command line of Antigravity (Google), version 1.1.22, and the credentials live in `jetski_state.pbtxt`. It does NOT read `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`: that variable does not appear among its strings, so Sailor's active profile does not move agy's home the way it moves codex's and claude's. The path is not declared here because the field wants a configuration path and this is the whole home; it is written here because whoever wants to redo the measurement needs it. The prompt goes in an argument, and `--print` sits in `args_before_prompt` because it must stay glued to the question: measured that `--print` takes the word following it as the question, and measured again that the `usage` options, appended after `ask`'s, landed right in between - `agy` answered«Error: --print took "--output-format" as its prompt» and the real text was ignored. `unusable_when` IS MEASURED, AND USED TO BE EMPTY. The measurement is the one codex was measured with: point `HOME` at an empty directory and run THE LINE SAILOR ACTUALLY COMPOSES — `agy --mode plan --output-format json --print "<question>"` — which without credentials calls no provider and costs nothing. Exit **1**, repeated twice identically: on stdout the JSON `{"status":"ERROR","response":"","error":"authentication failed or timed out",...}` with every token at zero, on stderr «Authentication required. Please visit the URL to log in:», the OAuth URL, «Waiting for authentication (timeout 60s)...» and finally «Error: authentication timed out.». The three entries in the list are those words, copied as they came out. WHAT WAS NOT MEASURED IS DECLARED TOO: the words agy uses to say it has run out of QUOTA stay unknown. Searched in `agy --help` and in every nested subcommand (`agy help <sub>`, `mcp` and `plugin` included), which name no limit; searched in the binary's string table, where capacity exhaustion appears only as an internal retry reason (`ShouldRetryModelCapacityExhausted`, `HasModelCapacityExhaustedReason`) and not as a printed message; and not provokable without spending the real quota. A quota exhaustion therefore still passes for an ordinary failure on agy. What the list covers is the other half of what `unusable_when` declares — missing credentials — exactly the half codex declares with its own 401. MIND WHAT A MEASUREMENT LIKE THIS COSTS: without credentials agy opens the browser on the OAuth URL and WAITS 60 SECONDS for a code on standard input before giving up. In a chain those 60 seconds are paid at every step. `refuses_without_prompt` is measured: `agy --mode plan --output-format json --print` exits 2 and prints «flag needs an argument: -print». THE SAME MEASUREMENT SHOWS WHY THE VERDICT CANNOT COME FROM THE EXIT CODE: the malformed line — `agy --mode plan --print --output-format json` — exits 2 as well, and says something else entirely («--print took "--output-format" as its prompt»). And `--help` proves nothing: `agy --mode nonsense-value --not-a-real-flag --help` exits 0, because it short-circuits before reading the arguments. NO `login_status` BLOCK, AND THIS IS WHAT WAS TRIED: `agy --help` lists eleven subcommands — `agent`, `agents`, `changelog`, `help`, `install`, `mcp`, `mic-serve`, `models`, `plugin`, `plugins`, `update` — and twenty-four options, and among them all neither `auth` nor `login` nor `logout` appears. The absence is written by staying silent and not by guessing — a wrong `logged_in_when` would declare an empty home authenticated, silently reinstating the defect the block closes. TWO SENTENCES THAT ACCOMPANIED THAT PARAGRAPH WERE REMOVED AT A MERGE, BECAUSE A MEASUREMENT FROM THE SAME DAY CONTRADICTS THEM: they said «no `unusable_when`, how it declares itself exhausted has not been seen» and «nobody even knows where agy keeps its configuration». The two measurements written above — the exit 1 with the three verbatim sentences, and the home `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli` — come from the other branch of the same day. Whoever picks the `login_status` search back up should start there: the home is known now, so it can be looked into; all that stays unknown is the words agy answers the question with.

ask_without_interaction.note: `run <model>` with the prompt on stdin answers once and exits; without stdin it opens a conversation

tools.note: With the service unreachable it prints a warning first: without `must_contain` that line would be recorded as if it were the version. `ask` runs the local coder model the strengths table names for mechanical work; the model is data here and `ollama pull` is the person's gesture. `--verbose` prints the counts on STDERR, hence `from`; the two patterns are the stats lines measured on 03/09/2026 with qwen2.5-coder:1.5b (`prompt eval count:    36 token(s)`, `eval count:           2 token(s)`; the second is anchored to a line start, or it would match inside the first). Measured the same day: the line composed WITHOUT a question exits 0 and prints nothing at all, so there are no refusal words to declare and `silent_without_prompt` says so. `data_pact` is `does_not_train` because nothing leaves the machine. No `model` pointer: the model is the one in `args`, and the row's model stays undeclared until a reader of the arguments exists.

tools.label: free-claude-code server

install.note: from the project's README on 03/09/2026: the script installs `fcc-server`; on macOS it also installs an application that starts it

tools.note: A program on this machine, connected and never built in: a server on localhost:8082 that speaks Claude Code's own protocol and answers with other companies' models, free or keyed. Read from its README on 03/09/2026, not measured here: it expects `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8082` and the fixed token `freecc`; its tiers are routed by `MODEL_OPUS`, `MODEL_SONNET`, `MODEL_HAIKU` and stay its own; its «connected accounts», which log in through another product's subscription, are never configured from Sailor. The way in is a Claude Code profile with this address as endpoint (`sailor profiles endpoint claude <name> http://localhost:8082 <var holding freecc> anthropic-messages`), still to verify against the token header the server checks. `data_pact` is unknown because the pact is the answering provider's, per model, and the server does not say which answered before the call.
